definitions.definition: Final destinations (like heaven or hell) that pull a person's moral state toward them over time, like a magnet pulling metal.
definitions.example: A marble rolling down a funnel is attracted to the bottom; your moral choices are attracted to either heaven or hell.

definitions.definition: A structural match between two different things, showing they work the same way even though they look different.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is isomorphic to the actual subway lines — the connections match even though the map is smaller.

definitions.definition: A basic assumption taken to be true without proof, used as a starting point for reasoning.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: A set of rules that describe how something changes over time, like a recipe for the future based on the present.
definitions.example: A bouncing ball is a dynamical system: its position and speed at each moment determine where it goes next.
definitions.first_appearance: A1 — Axiom: Moral destiny as dynamical system

definitions.definition: A pattern of results that has two separate peaks or clusters, instead of one big hump.
definitions.example: Heights of adult humans are unimodal (one peak), but if you mixed men and women's heights you'd get two peaks — that's bimodal.
definitions.first_appearance: A2 — Axiom: Bimodal distribution of final states

definitions.definition: A point in a system that is unstable — like the top of a hill between two valleys — where a tiny push sends you rolling down one side or the other.
definitions.example: Balancing a pencil on your finger: the balance point is a saddle — the slightest wobble makes it fall one way or the other.
definitions.first_appearance: C2 — Claim: Small perturbations near saddle produce dramatically different outcomes

definitions.definition: A small change or disturbance to a system that is otherwise stable or predictable.
definitions.example: A tiny nudge to a spinning top is a perturbation — it might make it wobble or fall over.
definitions.first_appearance: C2 — Claim: Small perturbations near saddle produce dramatically different outcomes

definitions.definition: Based on observation or experiment, not just theory or logic.
definitions.example: Saying 'water boils at 100°C' is empirical because you can test it with a thermometer.
definitions.first_appearance: C2 — Claim: Small perturbations near saddle produce dramatically different outcomes

definitions.definition: The process of checking whether something is correct or works as claimed.
definitions.example: A car company crash-tests a new model to validate its safety claims.
definitions.first_appearance: C2 — Claim: Small perturbations near saddle produce dramatically different outcomes

definitions.definition: A mathematical formula that describes how something grows quickly at first, then slows down as it hits a limit.
definitions.example: A population of rabbits in a field grows fast at first, but then slows as food runs out — that's logistic growth.
definitions.first_appearance: E1 — Evidence: Moral state evolution equation

definitions.definition: A pattern of results that has one single peak or cluster, like a bell curve.
definitions.example: Most people's test scores cluster around the average — that's a unimodal distribution.
definitions.first_appearance: E1 — Evidence: Moral state evolution equation

definitions.definition: The study of the final events in history and the ultimate destiny of humanity, like heaven, hell, and judgment.
definitions.example: Christians believe in an eschatology where Jesus returns and everyone is judged.

definitions.definition: A state that a system naturally moves toward over time, like a valley that a ball rolls into.
definitions.example: A pendulum eventually stops at the bottom — that resting point is an attractor.

definitions.definition: A map of all possible states a system can be in, showing how it can change over time.
definitions.example: For a bouncing ball, phase space includes its height and speed at every moment.

definitions.definition: A state where a system stops changing — it stays exactly the same forever unless something pushes it.
definitions.example: A marble at the bottom of a bowl is at a fixed point: it won't move unless you nudge it.

definitions.definition: A state that a system settles into and stays in, even if it gets a small push away.
definitions.example: A ball in a deep bowl: if you nudge it, it rolls back to the bottom — that's a stable attractor.

definitions.definition: A point that is balanced but any tiny push sends the system away from it — like a ball on top of a hill.
definitions.example: A pencil balanced on its tip: the slightest breeze makes it fall — that's an unstable saddle.

definitions.definition: The set of starting points that all lead to the same attractor, like the area of a hill that drains into one valley.
definitions.example: Any raindrop that falls on the east side of a mountain ridge flows into the Atlantic — that's its basin of attraction.

definitions.definition: The path a system follows over time as it changes from one state to another.
definitions.example: The arc of a basketball from your hands to the hoop is its trajectory.

definitions.definition: A measure of how aligned or unified something is — in this framework, how aligned a person is with God's will.
definitions.example: A choir singing in perfect harmony has high coherence; a crowd shouting randomly has low coherence.

definitions.definition: A number in the model that represents how much God's grace helps a person grow morally.
definitions.example: Think of it like a 'boost factor' — the higher it is, the faster someone can improve.

definitions.definition: How responsive a person is to moral influences — how easily they are affected by good or bad inputs.
definitions.example: A person with high moral sensitivity might feel guilty after telling a small lie; someone with low sensitivity might not care.

definitions.definition: The idea that something is completely destroyed or ceases to exist, rather than continuing in some form.
definitions.example: Some people believe hell is annihilation — the wicked simply stop existing, not suffer forever.

definitions.definition: The Christian belief that all humans are born with a tendency to sin, due to the 'Fall' of Adam and Eve.
definitions.example: The idea that people are naturally selfish, not perfectly good, is part of fallen anthropology.

definitions.definition: A concept in this framework that represents God's grace as a force that can change a person's moral direction.
definitions.example: Like a rescue boat that pulls a swimmer from a dangerous current into safe waters.

definitions.definition: The process of moving toward a single point or state over time.
definitions.example: As you zoom in on a fractal, the patterns converge to a repeating shape.

definitions.definition: Getting closer and closer to a value but never quite reaching it, like a line that approaches a curve forever.
definitions.example: A car slowing down to a stop asymptotically approaches zero speed — it gets very close but never exactly zero until it stops.

definitions.definition: Involving randomness or chance, not completely predictable.
definitions.example: Rolling dice is stochastic — you know the possible outcomes but not which one will happen.

definitions.definition: A system where everything is caused by what came before, with no randomness — the future is completely predictable if you know the rules.
definitions.example: A clock is deterministic: if you know how it's wound, you can predict exactly when it will tick.

definitions.definition: An outside input that pushes a system to change, like a hand pushing a swing.
definitions.example: Wind pushing a sailboat is a forcing function — it changes the boat's speed and direction.

definitions.definition: In Catholic belief, a temporary state after death where souls are purified before entering heaven.
definitions.example: Think of it like a shower after playing in mud — you're clean afterward, but it takes some time.

definitions.definition: A state that seems stable for a while but eventually changes to a more stable state, like a ball in a shallow dip that can roll out.
definitions.example: A soap bubble is metastable — it pops after a few seconds, but it looks stable until then.

definitions.definition: The belief that all people will eventually be saved and go to heaven, regardless of their actions or beliefs.
definitions.example: A universalist thinks even the worst person will end up in heaven after enough time.

definitions.definition: When a system takes a very long time to change near a tipping point, like a decision that takes forever to make.
definitions.example: A swing slows down near the top of its arc — that's critical slowing down before it swings back.

definitions.definition: When a system's state depends on its history — it doesn't snap back to where it started even if the cause is removed.
definitions.example: A paperclip bent out of shape doesn't spring back perfectly — it stays bent, showing hysteresis.

definitions.definition: A point where a small change causes a system to split into two very different behaviors.
definitions.example: Turning a faucet slowly: at first just drips, then suddenly a steady stream — that's a bifurcation.

definitions.definition: The idea that a scientific theory must be able to be proven wrong by evidence, or it's not scientific.
definitions.example: The claim 'all swans are white' can be falsified by finding one black swan.

definitions.definition: Growth that starts fast, then slows as it approaches a maximum limit, like filling a bathtub.
definitions.example: Bacteria in a petri dish grow fast at first, then slow as food runs out — that's logistic growth.

definitions.definition: The point where something cannot hold any more — it's full to the limit.
definitions.example: A sponge that can't soak up any more water has reached saturation.

definitions.definition: When a system's basic behavior doesn't change even if you tweak the rules a little bit.
definitions.example: A pendulum is structurally stable: even if you add a little friction, it still swings back and forth.

definitions.definition: A picture that shows all possible paths a system can take through its states over time.
definitions.example: A weather map with arrows showing wind directions is like a phase portrait of the atmosphere.

definitions.definition: The underlying material or medium that something exists in or is made of.
definitions.example: Soil is the substrate for plants — it's what they grow in.

definitions.definition: When a system not only returns to a stable state after a push, but gets closer and closer over time.
definitions.example: A marble in a sticky bowl: it rolls back to the bottom and eventually stops exactly there — that's asymptotic stability.

definitions.definition: When a process cannot be undone — you can't go back to how things were before.
definitions.example: Mixing milk into coffee is irreversible: you can't separate them again.
